LLMStructBench: Benchmarking Large Language Model Structured Data Extraction Thanks:  *Corresponding authors,
firstname.lastname@htw-berlin.de
KI‑Werkstatt / FB2, University of Applied Sciences Berlin

Sönke Tenckhoff*, Mario Koddenbrock, Erik Rodner* Affiliation: 
Abstract

We present LLMStructBench, a novel benchmark for evaluating llm on extracting structured data and generating valid json (json) outputs from natural-language text. Our open dataset comprises diverse, manually verified parsing scenarios of varying complexity and enables systematic testing across 22 models and five prompting strategies. We further introduce complementary performance metrics that capture both token-level accuracy and document-level validity, facilitating rigorous comparison of model, size, and prompting effects on parsing reliability.

In particular, we show that choosing the right prompting strategy is more important than standard attributes such as model size. This especially ensures structural validity for smaller or less reliable models but increase the number of semantic errors. Our benchmark suite is an step towards future research in the area of llm applied to parsing or etl (etl) applications.

I Introduction

Extracting structured information from natural language is a frequent requirement in domains such as human resources [1], finance [2], logistics, and e-commerce. llm are increasingly used for this task or related etl application, as for example highlighted by Xu et al. [3] in their survey on generative information extraction. However, their reliability in producing both syntactically valid and semantically correct outputs remains insufficiently understood. Lu et al. [4] demonstrate that even state-of-the-art models often fail to generate fully schema-compliant and semantically faithful json outputs. Yet many downstream systems depend on receiving a complete and accurate object on the first attempt, making both structure and content essential [5].

To address this, we created a benchmark of realistic scenarios, each linked to a predefined json schema and paired with natural language messages that contain all required information.

Our dataset was synthetically generated with controlled prompting and then manually verified, removing or correcting cases where the text and schema did not align. It covers a range of complexity from flat key–value pairs to deeply nested structures. This design allows systematic testing of different models and prompting strategies while keeping gt consistent and unambiguous.

In our evaluation, we focus exclusively on open-source llm. This choice reflects typical deployment constraints in data integration and etl workflows, where sensitive or proprietary information cannot be shared with commercial cloud APIs. By benchmarking openly available models, we aim to provide realistic insights for practitioners who require locally deployable and privacy-preserving solutions.

For completeness, we additionally include the proprietary GPT-4o model as a reference point. Its inclusion allows us to gauge how far open-weight systems have progressed toward commercial performance levels, without changing our overall focus on openly available models.

The contributions of our paper can be summarized as follows:

  1. 1.

    We present an open dataset for structured parsing evaluation, comprising 995 manually verified samples across multiple use-case scenarios. It is specifically designed for JSON outputs and the application of llms (section III).

  2. 2.

    We introduce quality metrics that allow for capturing syntactic and semantic errors both on a character-/ and the document-level (section IV).

  3. 3.

    In our work, we are able to compare 22 state-of-the-art llm with different prompting strategies offering immediate results and recommendations for practitioners (section VI and section VII).

II Related Work

Recent studies explore two complementary directions for improving the reliability of structured outputs from llm: (i) the development of benchmarks and decoding frameworks to enforce schema compliance [6, 4] and, (ii) the design of prompting strategies and workflows to improve extraction accuracy under realistic text conditions [7, 8, 3].

Benchmarks and schema-constrained decoding. Geng et al. [6] introduce JSONSchemaBench, a large benchmark of real-world json Schemas that evaluate constrained decoding engines across efficiency, coverage of json schema features, and output quality. Their results indicate that grammar- or schema-constrained decoding can accelerate generation and improve downstream task accuracy, yet support for advanced schema features differs substantially between frameworks. Our work is similar to their paper by measuring not only document validity, but also semantic extraction quality. In contrast to [6], which focuses on engine compliance under given schema, we analyze how prompting strategies and model families trade off between perfect structure and correct values in an end-to-end ie setting.

Synthetic benchmark generation from structured data. StructText [9] proposes an automatic table-to-text pipeline that uses existing tables as gt to synthesize narratives and then evaluate text-to-table extraction along factuality, hallucination, coherence, and numeric or temporal accuracy. The authors find that models preserve numeric and temporal content, but often produce narratives that hinder machine extractability. Our dataset targets naturally occurring messages rather than llm-synthesized narratives, which reduces the risk that coherence artifacts of synthetic text bias extraction results. At the same time, our analysis echoes their observation that accessibility for downstream parsing is as important as factuality.

Domain benchmarks for structured spatial outputs. Li et al. [10] present a benchmark for GeoJSON generation and a hybrid R-tree-enhanced workflow that improves spatial coherence. While their findings generalize the need for structure-aware workflows, their scope is geospatial. Our benchmark complements this by focusing on general json key–value extraction in heterogeneous messages and by reporting micro-averaged validity to reflect practical parser robustness.

Prompting strategies for structured ie. Li et al. [7] propose a two-step “Generate & Organize” prompting scheme that first elicits free-form answers and then organizes them into the target structure with a task-specific clean-up stage. This approach reduces formatting errors that often occur when content extraction and formatting are requested at once. Our experiments corroborate the central premise: separating schema conformance from semantic correctness can change the error profile.

Structured outputs in competitive pipelines. Pradhan et al. [8] demonstrate that enforcing a fixed json schema during generation, combined with lightweight domain-specific validation rules, can yield top leaderboard results without task-specific fine-tuning on several health ie tasks. Their approach constrains the model to produce outputs that directly match the required structure. This concept, often referred to as schema-driven prompting, provides the model with an explicit output schema or example object within the prompt. Our evaluation extends this idea to a broader range of open-source models and analyzes how such schema enforcement influences different error types, including mk (mk)s and incorrect values.

Surveys and practical extraction workflows. The survey by Xu et al. [3] synthesizes progress in generative ie and highlights persistent challenges such as misalignment between natural language and structured targets, hallucination, and high computational cost. Our results quantify this misalignment for json outputs by separating document validity from extraction accuracy.

Positioning. Across these threads, prior work either stresses schema compliance under constrained decoding [6] or shows that careful prompting can make outputs parsable without training [7, 8]. We contribute a complementary benchmark and analysis centered on json parsing fidelity in everyday email communication, a common medium for automating administrative and business processes. Our evaluation quantifies how prompting strategies redistribute errors between structural validity and value correctness and introduces metrics that capture both dimensions. This addresses a gap identified by Kashyap et al. [9] and Xu et al. [3], namely that factual accuracy alone is insufficient unless information remains accessible to automated parsers.

III Dataset and Benchmark

The proposed benchmark dataset is designed to evaluate llm on structured ie and json generation tasks across diverse, realistic communication scenarios, something we will refer to as use-cases in the following. These use-cases are inspired by typical email-based workflows in domains such as IT support, human resources, or project management—settings in which automation often relies on transforming free-text messages into structured, machine-readable records. Table I provides a full list of all use-cases considered.

Benchmark setup. Figure 1 illustrates the inference-time setup of our benchmark. Each model receives a natural-language message, a representative example pair (text and reference json), and the corresponding json schema that defines the required structure. It is instructed to return a single json object adhering to this schema. The generated output is then compared to the validated gt object to measure both structural validity and semantic accuracy. Further details on the evaluation procedure are provided in Section IV.

Scenario and dataset structure. Each benchmark scenario (use case) defines a self-contained extraction task and provides all necessary components for reproducible testing. A scenario specification includes:

  • •

    a short description of the task

  • •

    the corresponding json schema defining key names, data types, and nesting depth,

  • •

    example input (text) and output (json) pairs

  • •

    prompt templates for generating synthetic input text from structured data (email generation) and for extracting structured data from text (conversion)

  • •

    a total of 199 validated test cases.

Each individual test case then links one natural-language message with its corresponding schema-conform ground-truth object. The schema remains fixed within a scenario, while the natural-language formulations vary to reflect realistic message diversity.

Dataset composition. The complete dataset covers five use cases of varying structural complexity, resulting in 995 total tests. As shown in Table I, the scenarios range from shallow key–value mappings (Support tickets) to nested object arrays (Loan requests), enabling analysis of model robustness across different structure depths. Two exemplary input-output pairs can be found in Appendix -B.

III-A Synthetic Data Generation

For each use case, synthetic test cases were generated using GPT-4o. The process first produced fully populated json objects that followed the scenario-specific schema. Using the email generation prompt, these json objects were transformed into realistic and varying natural language messages, for example vacation requests, expense reports, or order confirmations. This ensured that the dataset covered diverse writing styles and lexical variations while maintaining a one-to-one correspondence between the gt json and the generated text.

To introduce variety, prompt instructions enforced randomization of entity names, dates, numerical values and other scenario-specific fields. This allowed the creation of many unique instances for each use case, covering both simple and highly nested data structures as displayed in Table I.

III-B Dataset Verification and Cleaning

The initial dataset was manually reviewed to ensure correctness. Faulty scenarios, where the gt json systematically deviated from the information present in the corresponding text, were removed entirely. In cases where only specific entries were affected, for example a single missing value repeated across multiple instances, corrections were applied by hand.

After these steps, all retained examples contain:

  • •

    a complete and schema-valid json object

  • •

    a corresponding text message reflecting all information present in the JSON object

  • •

    no systematic mismatches between the two representations

III-C Final Dataset Composition

The cleaned dataset covers multiple complexity levels, from flat key–value structures to deeper nested hierarchies with lists and objects. Scenarios include realistic domains such as human resources, project management, IT support, logistics and e-commerce. This diversity allows the benchmark to assess both the syntactic reliability and the semantic accuracy of model outputs under controlled and realistic conditions. We also experimented with use cases and schema that involved more nested json-objects, however, this did not result in even medium quality generated examples and have been therefore skipped. Often times the generation of the email was missing out on many crucial values from the ground-truth base object.

IV Quality Metrics and Evaluation Strategy

To evaluate outputs against the gt, we perform a recursive comparison and classify discrepancies into:

  • •

    mk (mk): Key–value pairs present in the reference but absent in the model output.

  • •

    mv (mv): Values that are absent, either because their key is missing entirely or because the key is present but its value is null.

  • •

    wv (wv): Values that differ, subdivided into:

    • –

      Value deviation: Both reference and candidate are strings; measured by Levenshtein distance.

    • –

      Value error: Same primitive type but different content.

    • –

      Coercible mismatch: Stringified forms match, but the underlying types differ.

    • –

      Type error: Neither same type nor coercible to the same string.

IV-A Performance Metrics

Micro-averaged F1 (F​1microF1_{\text{micro}}). We treat each key:value pair as a classification instance and measure precision/recall over all instances in the corpus. Because downstream consumers usually care more about the correctness of the produced values than about the mere presence of a key, we split the metric into two parts and mix them linearly

F​1micro\displaystyle F1_{\text{micro}} =α​F​1keys+(1−α)​F​1values\displaystyle=\alpha\,F1_{\text{keys}}+(1-\alpha)\,F1_{\text{values}} (1)

with a key weight of α=0.25\alpha=0.25 (ref. IV-B). Concretely:

  • •

    Key component (F​1keysF1_{\text{keys}}) counts true-positive keys (present and unique), false-positives (extraneous keys) and false-negatives (mks).

  • •

    Value component (F​1valuesF1_{\text{values}}) evaluates value correctness with a nuanced credit system. It rewards exact matches fully and penalizes wrong or missing values. For mismatches, it distinguishes between error types:

    • –

      It grants partial credit for coercible mismatches (e.g., string "42" vs. integer 4242) and for value deviations in strings, where credit is proportional to string similarity (inverse Levenshtein distance).

    • –

      It actively penalizes string comparisons that are drastically different, discouraging nonsensical outputs.

    • –

      It assigns zero credit for hard type errors and value errors, treating them as complete failures.

A formal definition of the full scoring function, including fuzzy value matching and weighting constants, is provided in Appendix -A. In essence, the metric rewards fully correct pairs, grants graded credit for close or type-compatible values, and penalizes missing or nonsensical entries, yielding a single bounded score F​1micro∈[0,1]F1_{\text{micro}}\!\in\![0,1].

Document success ( doc (doc)micro{}_{\text{micro}}). Token-level scores can still be high when every document has a few small errors, yet many real-world pipelines accept only fully valid JSON. Therefore we add a document success term

D​O​Cmicro= # Correct  # Tests ​(1− # Failed  # Tests ),\displaystyle DOC_{\text{micro}}\;=\;\frac{\text{\,\#\,Correct\,}}{\text{\,\#\,Tests\,}}\Bigl(1-\frac{\text{\,\#\,Failed\,}}{\text{\,\#\,Tests\,}}\Bigr), (2)

i.e. the share of completely correct generations tempered by the share of outright failures (empty output, unparsable json, fatal schema violation). It, too, lies in [0,1][0,1]. This metric corresponds to document‑level validity or schema adherence in structured output benchmarks [6]. It captures brittleness that token‑level scores can hide.

IV-B Combined Rating

To rank models on a single, easily interpretable scale we combine token-level accuracy with document-level validity into one composite score, which we derive from F​1microF1_{\text{micro}} and docmicro{}_{\text{micro}} scores.

Score =(1−λ)​F​1micro+λ​D​O​Cmicro\displaystyle=(1-\lambda)\,F1_{\text{micro}}\;+\;\lambda\,DOC_{\text{micro}} (3)

with a weight of λ=0.5\lambda=0.5, as motivated in the paragraph below.

Document‑level validity matches the notion of validity used by JSONSchemaBench for schema adherence under constrained decoding [6]. Micro‑averaged extraction F1 follows the practice in ie surveys and shared tasks where per field correctness is aggregated over all instances [3, 8].

Choice of weights. We selected the two free hyper-parameters empirically, guided by practitioner feedback:

  1. 1.

    Key to Value weight α=0.25\alpha=0.25. A low weight on key-level F1 reflects the fact that getting a value correct is typically more critical than getting its key correct. Furthermore, a mk is implicitly penalized twice: once in the key-F1 score (as a false negative) and again in the value-F1 score (since its value is also missing). By down-weighting the key component, we heavily prioritize models that produce correct values in the correct locations, as a wrong value can silently corrupt downstream logic, whereas an extraneous or mk is often less severe.

  2. 2.

    Document to F1 weight λ=0.5\lambda=0.5. In early experiments (0.3≤λ≤0.70.3\leq\lambda\leq 0.7) we observed that scores below 0.40.4 de-emphasised outright failures (models that emit markdown instead of json still ranked mid-table) while scores above 0.60.6 masked the nuanced differences between good and excellent token-level accuracy. A neutral split (half structure, half content) preserves sensitivity in both regimes.

Because each term is differentiable and independently reported, practitioners can still drill down into why a model under-performs. Whether due to structural brittleness (low docmicro{}_{\text{micro}}) or semantic drift (low F​1microF1_{\text{micro}}).

V Model and Prompting Techniques

V-A Models Used in this Study

We selected twenty-two model variants from five families, spanning from 0.60.6 to 7070 billion parameters:

  • •

    Qwen3 [11]: Qwen3:0.6b (0.6 B), Qwen3:1.7b (1.7 B), Qwen3:4b (4 B), Qwen3:8b (8 B), Qwen3:14b (14 B), Qwen3:32b (32 B).

  • •

    Phi [12]: Phi3:3.8b (3.8 B), Phi3:14b (14 B), Phi3.5:3.8b (3.8 B), Phi4-mini:3.8b (3.8 B), Phi4:14b (14 B).

  • •

    Gemma3 [13]: gemma3:1b (1 B), gemma3:12b (12 B), gemma3:27b (27 B).

  • •

    Deepseek-R1 [14]: Deepseek-R1:1.5b (1.5 B), Deepseek-R1:7b (7 B), Deepseek-R1:8b (8 B), Deepseek-R1:14b (14 B), Deepseek-R1:32b (32 B), Deepseek-R1:70b (70 B).

  • •

    LLama3 [15]: Llama3.1:70b (70 B), Llama3.3:70b (70 B).

In addition, we include GPT-4o as a closed-weight reference model. It is evaluated under the same benchmark conditions to contextualize the performance of open models. Since its parameter count and detailed training data remain undisclosed, it is excluded from size-based and combined analyses. The model evaluation serves solely as an upper-bound reference rather than part of the open-source comparison pool.

Besides that, the selection of open sourc models allows us to assess how both architecture and scale affect json parsing performance and data quality.

V-B Prompting Techniques

To identify the most reliable way to get well-formed json from our models, we evaluated five different prompting configurations (see Table II). Each configuration varies along two axes:

  1. 1.

    whether we set the Ollama API format parameter (either to the literal string ”json” or to a full json-Schema object) and

  2. 2.

    whether we explicitly instruct the model, via system and user prompts, to follow a provided schema and an example json structure

By comparing these five conditions, we can disentangle the impact of API-level json enforcement from explicit prompt-level schema guidance on the consistency and validity of the returned json.

V-C Prompting Technique Evaluation

To determine which prompting strategy yields the most reliable json generation across models, we computed a premature performance score for each strategy by weighting outcomes from the evaluation results. Specifically, each strategy was scored using a simple linear metric that prioritizes correctly parsed outputs and penalizes various types of errors with different severity:

  • •

    Correct: Flawless generations are rewarded with
    10 Points per test-case. This is rewarded with a large amount of points, as we really take emphasis on consistency in data extraction.

  • •

    Mistakes: Value deviation or extra keys are penalized with
    -1 Point per occurrence. Occurrences of mistakes enforce the need for data validation through other means in the downstream pipeline.

  • •

    Errors: Missing values or keys are penalized with
    -2 Points per occurrence. They cost double the amount as mistakes, as they are really missing information, that need substitution later.

  • •

    Failures: A failed generation is penalized with
    -15 Points per test-case. Generally all scenarios and tests of the benchmark have a clear solution, so failing to return a JSON-Object in the first place is penalized servilely.

This weighted scoring scheme reflects the qualitative differences between error types and their impact on usability in downstream applications. For each model, the strategy with the highest score was selected as the ”winner” for that model. In cases of a tie, all top-scoring strategies were counted. This procedure allowed us to tally how often each prompting configuration produced the most favorable result across the full model pool. It also allows for discovering shortcomings of individual models or entire model families, regarding specific prompting strategies.

VI Experiments

We structure our evaluation into three stages. First, we compare all prompting strategies using the parsing metric introduced in Section VI-A, and rank them in Table IV.

Second, in Section VI-B, we study the two best strategies across model families and sizes, evaluating both extraction accuracy and document validity via F​1microF1_{\text{micro}} and docmicro{}_{\text{micro}} (Section IV-B).

Finally, Section VI-C presents a consolidated leaderboard of all evaluated models, shown in Table V.

VI-A Impact of the Prompting Strategy on Parsing performance

We begin with one of the lower-ranked models, which struggled to produce a sufficient number of flawless json results even under the more structured prompting setups. In Figure 2 you can see the evaluation of the Phi3 model with 3.8b parameters. The results are separated to display the capability of the selected model, to return a valid json object for each strategy of prompting. In this first evaluation, we don’t take into account the quality of content of the answer itself, but rather focus only on the possibility of parsing the answer to a valid json-Object.

The model displayed (Phi3 - 3.8b), together with its successor (Phi3.5 - 3.8b), is among the worst performing models within this category. Across all prompting strategies, there are at least some occasions where tests fail completely. This is visualized by the red bars on the chart. On the other hand, the green bar represents all test counts where the model responded with a clean answer, that was successfully parsed to a json-Object without any additional tweaks.

A count of Extracted parsing succeeded is added every time the model returns more context around the wanted json-Object. Here, we try to use regex to extract the relevant section, containing the json-formatted string from the larger text-answer.

To evaluate a model’s capability to also extract the right information from a given text, again, compared by different prompting strategies, we have to look at another chart. On Figure 3 we compare not only parsing success, but this time how many test cases had a perfect match of the json return object to gt. This count is destincly low for all prompting-strategies with the Phi3 - 3.8b model.

We also notice quite large bars for mistakes (orange) which indicates mismatches between json-values or additional key/value pairs. These are not as severe as the errors (gray) which indicate when a key, or value is completely missing from the language model’s response.

When comparing the results based on prompting techniques for Phi3, it demonstrated the most promising performance applying the PJ+-prompting strategy. While it produced 298298 perfect json objects and incurred 130130 errors, its notably absence of failed test cases demonstrates the baseline of our prompting technique selection process.

After evaluating prompting techniques for all chosen models, we end up with a table (Table III) of most promising prompting techniques for further testing and evaluation.

Based on this result and our proposed metric for scoring the different performances based on prompting strategy, we are able to deviate following strategy ranking (Table IV). It clearly shows P-strategy as best performing one with a count of 1111 favorable model applications, with PJ+ as runner-up.

This is also reflected in the raw evaluation data in Table III, as both P and PJ+ have the highest count of entirely correct results. Prompting with P strategy exhibits an unusual high count of failed test cases. This is down to the Phi3-family really struggling with this specific prompting type. All other model families display a lower average count of failures using the P-prompting technique. While the P strategy almost shows double the amount of errors, compared to PJ+, it’s still in the lower range compared to other strategies. Additionally it is the best option for less severe mistakes with 14.17114.171 combined occurrences over 995995 performed tests.

Going forward, we are focusing on comparing results for both strategies proven to be relevant.

VI-B Impact of Model Size on Value Extraction Performance

Now, that we have established the prominent prompting strategies P and PJ+ we can take a look at the different parsing performances by model family and respective size variation. In Figure 4 we can observe the performance of all Gemma3-model size variations. The graph clearly displays the steep improvement from a really small model size (e.g. 1​B1B parameters) to the next bigger variant (12​B12B parameters). This is expressed by the reduction of errors and mistakes, at the same time as the response count of perfect matches with the gt json increases.

When we compare the second biggest, to the largest model variant, we assert only a small improvement in the increase of success counts as well as the reduction of failure, errors and mistakes. This is to be expected, as the model size only doubles from the second to the last model variant, while the second to the first is an approximated 1212-times increase in size.

While the comparison of model performance by the current four metrics, success, fail, error and mistake is reasonable for settling on a fitting prompting strategy, it isn’t very well suited for the evaluation of model families including higher counts of model variants.

Therefore we apply the overall performance rating that we proposed in a previous section (ref. Section IV-B). It gives us one single score for each model variant, that is derived from the accuracy of extracting correct data (F​1microF1_{\text{micro}}-Score ref. Section IV-A), as well from the models ability to return parse-able and flawless json objects in the first place (docmicro{}_{\text{micro}}-Score ref. Section IV-A). For the Gemma3 family the overall scoring is shown in Figure 5, still separated into F​1microF1_{\text{micro}} and docmicro{}_{\text{micro}}.

We can clearly observe the relation between the low count of flawless results (9898 out of 955955) of the 11b parameter variant in Figure 4 to the bad performing docmicro{}_{\text{micro}}-score (0.10.1) in Figure 5. A perfect docmicro{}_{\text{micro}}-Score can only be achieved when all json-Objects returned without any deviations to the gt. Another observation between the error and score plots is the reduction of errors and mistakes with increasing model size to a slightly improving F​1microF1_{\text{micro}}-score. This micro averaged composite score also takes partially correct results, like string overlaps through Levenshtein-distance, or variable type deviations into account, thus dampening the impact of change in the raw count of error occurrences over model size.

As a next step, the two metrics (F​1microF1_{\text{micro}} subsection IV-A and docmicro{}_{\text{micro}} subsection IV-A) that make up our overall scoring, let us determine the consistency in accuracy and document level correctness. Figure 6 displays the distribution of results for the Deepseek-R1-family.

We calculated the F​1microF1_{\text{micro}}-score for every single test case and look at the distribution of results. As the docmicro{}_{\text{micro}}-score is a document level score, it can not be calculated for each test, but instead will be calculated separately for each of the eight test scenarios per model testing extend. We observe an steady accumulation of high F​1microF1_{\text{micro}}-scores, represented by the average low height of blue boxes. This tells us, that model accuracy is fairly consistent between different extraction task and model size variants.

When we take a look at the docmicro{}_{\text{micro}}-score distribution on the other hand, we do not only observe quite a large variance, but also an increase of variance with a rise in model size. Surprisingly, the same trend is visible with the Qwen3 and Gemma3 model-families. In these cases, with larger model size, the median docmicro{}_{\text{micro}} score rises, but the variance in score is also becoming larger. The cause for this behavior could be down to an incompatibility of prompting strategy with each model family, as we are currently looking at results using P-type prompting. For the Deepseek-R1 model in specific, there are some jumps in document level correctness variance every other model size. This can be attributed to the two model-families, (Llama and Qwen), Deepseek is derived from, each reacting differently to the applied prompting strategy. To find out if this is the case, we take a look at Figure 7 implementing the PJ+-strategy.

Starting with the F​1microF1_{\text{micro}}-score again, we notice almost no difference, but only minor improvements between the two charts. But comparing the docmicro{}_{\text{micro}}-score reveals, that Deepseek-R1 does perform way more predictable in terms of correct to failed json results with PJ+ prompting. Even tough a slight variance in median values between the different model size variants can still be observed, the spread of test scores has generally declined for all model size variants. This confirms, that just changing the prompting strategy, can improve docmicro{}_{\text{micro}} performance greatly with model families, derived from multiple, different base models.

When we test and score all selected models, it results in the model score list Table V.

The small Phi-family models generally do not perform good in this evaluation which is down to their incompatibility with the P-prompting strategy as previously noted. We can observe some outliers with Phi3 - 14b, Phi4 - 14b and Phi4-mini - 3.8b, which rank in the middle of our list, implying a better performance with the selected prompting method than their other family members.

Surprisingly, the leaderboard shows no strict monotonic relationship between parameter count and overall score. While the very top tier is still dominated by large-capacity systems (≥70\geq{}70 B), the correlation flattens quickly, confirming prior observations that structured-output reliability is often shaped more by prompting and schema handling than by scale alone [4, 6, 3].

  • •

    Gemma3 – 12b punches above its weight, landing in the top three and even eclipsing several 70 B models. This mirrors findings from independent structured-output benchmarks, where smaller, well-tuned models achieved accuracy comparable to much larger ones, suggesting that data curation and architectural efficiency can outweigh raw size [10].

  • •

    Qwen3 – 1.7b is only one-tenth the size of the front-runners yet sits comfortably mid-table, outscoring half of the 14–32 B class. Similar to the conclusions of Lu et al. [4], who show that model scale alone does not ensure schema-compliant JSON generation, our results highlight the effectiveness of careful prompt alignment even for compact models.

  • •

    Conversely, Deepseek-R1 – 32b lags behind smaller peers, illustrating that additional parameters alone do not guarantee gains with the chosen P-prompting strategy. This also aligns with prior benchmark analyses where performance differences between decoding frameworks and prompting techniques exceeded those between model sizes [6].

Taken together, these outliers suggest that pre-training data quality, instruction tuning, and architectural tweaks can outweigh brute-force scale for this particular extraction task. Comparable effects were reported in synthetic and structured-generation studies, where post-processing design and two-step prompting strategies improved structural validity more than model enlargement [9, 7].

The figure shows a steady, largely log-linear improvement in F​1microF1_{\text{micro}} as model size increases. In contrast, docmicro{}_{\text{micro}} exhibits greater variance, particularly among smaller models, and highlights the notable outliers discussed earlier. This suggests that while accuracy generally scales with model size, the document-level score is more sensitive to prompting strategy and model-prompt interaction. To further assess this observation, we examine Figure 9, which presents results for the second-best prompting method, PJ+.

The F​1microF1_{\text{micro}} results closely match the previous prompting setup, with the exception of the Phi models (Phi3-3.8B and Phi3.5-3.8B), which show reduced accuracy. In contrast, the distribution of docmicro{}_{\text{micro}} scores shifts notably. No clear monotonic trend appears across model sizes, and the greatest variation now occurs in mid-sized models rather than at the small end. This further supports our finding that accuracy scales primarily with model size, whereas document-level reliability depends strongly on the combination of model and prompting strategy rather than scale alone.

VI-C Detailed Failure Analysis

Another interesting point of investigation is the distribution of json error types per count of performed tests. This will give us an insight, on what kind errors were made and on how many tests a specific combination of errors occurred. To visualize the overlapping distributions, we opted to imply a venn plot. On Figure 10, the error types mk, wv, mv are shown for the Deepseek-R1 model family, thrown using the P-prompting strategy. An overlap of two bubbles represents, that both mistakes were made at least once in the same test. As only one count of error category is counted per single test, the combined value of all bubbles in one plot is equal to the count of all tests (995995) minus the individual failed and flawless results per model. For each checkpoint the count of runs that could exhibit any error are calculated as follows.

Nerr=Ntests−(Nperfect+Nfailed),N_{\text{err}}=N_{\text{tests}}-\bigl(N_{\text{perfect}}+N_{\text{failed}}\bigr),

The Deepseek-R1 series shows a clear trajectory under the P-prompting setup. At 1.5b parameters the model still drops required keys frequently, making schema violations a noticeable portion of its failures. That problem is largely resolved by the time the network reaches 7b, where only three such cases remain, and it effectively disappears at 8b and beyond, with at most a single omission recorded for any larger checkpoint.

Once keys are reliably present, the dominant issue becomes incorrect content. wv errors start at 389389 cases for 1.5b, climb steadily with scale and peak at 632632 for the 32b checkpoint before edging down to 501501 at 70b. Even the largest model therefore produces at least one wrong field in roughly half of the test runs, indicating that value fidelity, rather than structural compliance, is the main bottleneck.

Purely mv slightly decline from 4646 at 1.5b to 1212 at 70b, tracking a similar drop in the overlapping missing & wrong region. The overlap never vanishes entirely, implying that the two error modes share a common source of confusion about the required content and structure.

In summary, key omissions vanish once the model reaches mid-scale, but incorrect or absent values persist. Larger parameter counts beyond roughly 14b offer only marginal gains for value accuracy, so further improvement is likely to depend on specialized conditioning or post-generation validation rather than additional scale alone.

Switching from the P to the PJ+ template on Figure 11 changes the error mix more than the error volume. To better understand the differences in error spread, we consult the Table VI that shows NerrN_{\text{err}} for each model and the two selected prompting options combined with inclusive incidence of the three error classes. Individual error shares are calculated relative to NerrN_{\text{err}}. As there is overlap of error types in between a single tests, the sum of all percentages can exceed 100%100\,\%.

Under the P prompt, mk errors still account for 36.8%36.8\,\% of the error pool at 1.5b but drop below 1.2%1.2\,\% by 7b, while mv persists between 4.8,%4.8,\% and 18.9%18.9\,\% across the model size range. Inclusive counting shows that wv already describes most imperfect runs, reaching 97​–​98%97\text{–}98\,\% on the larger checkpoints.

For the 1.5b checkpoint, replacing P with PJ+ lowers NerrN_{\text{err}} from 790790 to 605605 (−23%-23\,\%), because many outputs that previously failed the schema test now pass. For all larger checkpoints NerrN_{\text{err}} rises modestly by 22 to 1313 per-cent. Since PJ+ template leaves no run unparseable yet converts some formerly perfect parses into wv cases (e.g. 433433 perfect runs at 14b under P shrink to 364364 under PJ+).

In practical terms, PJ+ guarantees a complete json structure with the Deepseek-R1 model family but redirects almost every remaining uncertainty into field content. The result is a higher count of semantically flawed values despite the absence of structural faults, shifting the downstream burden from schema repair to semantic validation.

A comparison with the top-performing closed- and open-weight systems is shown in Table VII, where GPT-4o and Gemma3 - 27b exhibit a similar dominance of wv errors under both prompting strategies.

VII Conclusion

While GPT-4o was added as a closed-weight reference, it did not exhibit a clear advantage over the best open-source models (e.g. Gemma3 - 27B), reinforcing the practical competitiveness of deployable open systems.

The experiments further prove that prompting strategy and model architecture are at least as important as model scale for json parsing tasks.

  • •

    P strategy often yields the best overall balance of accuracy and validity for well-aligned models but can fail catastrophically for some families (e.g., Phi).

  • •

    PJ+ strategy is the safest choice for ensuring parseable outputs, especially for small or structurally unreliable models, but this comes at the cost of increased semantic errors.

  • •

    Model size helps, particularly for improving value accuracy (F​1micro)\bigl(F1_{\text{micro}}\bigr), but docmicro{}_{\text{micro}} is more sensitive to prompt–model compatibility than to scale.

  • •

    wv errors remain the primary bottleneck across all configurations, suggesting that post-generation semantic validation or fine-tuning is needed for further gains.

  • •

    Optimal performance is achieved by matching the prompting approach to the model family, not by relying solely on large parameter counts.

As shown in Table VIII, we summarize the best-performing prompting strategy for each evaluated model family and size, along with their composite scores under both the P and PJ+ prompting strategy, the dominant error types, and notable observations. This overview condenses the experimental findings by linking model scale, architecture, and prompt design to observed strengths and weaknesses. It highlights cases where smaller models achieve competitive performance, where prompting choice has a decisive impact on document validity (D​O​Cmicro)\bigl(DOC_{\text{micro}}\bigr), and where specific error types, such as wv, persist regardless of structural correctness.

-A Formal definition of the micro-F1 metric

For completeness, we restate the exact formulation of the micro-averaged score F​1microF1_{\text{micro}} used throughout this work.

F​1micro\displaystyle F1_{\text{micro}} =α​F​1keys+(1−α)​F​1values,α=0.25,\displaystyle=\alpha\,F1_{\text{keys}}+(1-\alpha)\,F1_{\text{values}},\qquad\alpha=0.25, (4)

where each component is defined as a standard F1F_{1}–measure:

F​1keys\displaystyle F1_{\text{keys}} =2​Pkeys​RkeysPkeys+Rkeys,\displaystyle=\frac{2\,P_{\text{keys}}\,R_{\text{keys}}}{P_{\text{keys}}+R_{\text{keys}}}, F​1values\displaystyle F1_{\text{values}} =2​Pvalues​RvaluesPvalues+Rvalues,\displaystyle=\frac{2\,P_{\text{values}}\,R_{\text{values}}}{P_{\text{values}}+R_{\text{values}}}, (5)
Pkeys\displaystyle P_{\text{keys}} =T​PkT​Pk+F​Pk,\displaystyle=\frac{TP_{k}}{TP_{k}+FP_{k}}, Pvalues\displaystyle P_{\text{values}} =T​PvT​Pv+F​Pv,\displaystyle=\frac{TP_{v}}{TP_{v}+FP_{v}}, (6)
Rkeys\displaystyle R_{\text{keys}} =T​PkT​Pk+F​Nk,\displaystyle=\frac{TP_{k}}{TP_{k}+FN_{k}}, Rvalues\displaystyle R_{\text{values}} =T​PvT​Pv+F​Nv.\displaystyle=\frac{TP_{v}}{TP_{v}+FN_{v}}. (7)

The value-level true positives T​PvTP_{v} incorporate partial credit for near matches:

T​Pv\displaystyle TP_{v} =Nv−F​Nv−(Etype+Evalue+Ecoerce+Edev)\displaystyle=N_{v}-FN_{v}-(E_{\text{type}}+E_{\text{value}}+E_{\text{coerce}}+E_{\text{dev}}) (8)
+∑i=1NlevC(li)+βEcoerce,\displaystyle\quad+\sum_{i=1}^{N_{\text{lev}}}C(l_{i})+\beta\,E_{\text{coerce}},

with β=0.2\beta=0.2 denoting the similarity gain for coercible mismatches. The fuzzy credit function C⁡(l)C(l) depends on the normalized Levenshtein distance ll between reference and prediction:

C⁡(l)={1,l≤Lgood,γ⁡(1−l),Lgood<l<Lbad,pbad,l≥Lbad,\displaystyle C(l)=\begin{cases}1,&l\leq L_{\text{good}},\\[2.0pt] \gamma\,(1-l),&L_{\text{good}}<l<L_{\text{bad}},\\[2.0pt] p_{\text{bad}},&l\geq L_{\text{bad}},\end{cases} (9)

where γ=0.5\gamma=0.5 controls the weight for approximate matches, Lgood=0.1L_{\text{good}}=0.1, Lbad=2.0L_{\text{bad}}=2.0, and pbad=−1p_{\text{bad}}=-1 applies a penalty for hopelessly wrong strings.
